hints: Focus on the different personalities of the halogens, chlorine is the bleaching and sterilising one, while bromine is strongly linked to fire control.
Notice that bleach, PVC and CFCs all have chloro in their names or formulas, like $\text{NaClO}$, poly(chloroethene) and chlorofluorocarbons.
Connect bromine to brominated organic compounds and halons that are added to plastics and extinguishers to slow down burning.
walkthrough:
**Recall the big uses of chlorine**

Chlorine is the workhorse for bleaching, cleaning and chlorinated polymers. Think bleach, killing microbes in water, PVC and old CFCs.

Key link to remember:
$$\text{Cl}_2 \text{ makes bleach, } \text{CFCs and PVC}$$

**Recall the big uses of bromine**

Bromine is much less used for bleaching. Its key industrial role is in brominated flame retardants for plastics and fabrics, and in halon fire extinguishers.

Key link to remember:
$$\text{Br}_2 \text{ makes flame retardants and halons}$$

**Match the list to bromine**

Options about bleaches, CFCs and PVC all point to chlorine chemistry. Only the fire-related option fits the classic bromine use, so that is the one to choose.

options.A: This is a classic use of chlorine, not bromine. Chlorine with sodium hydroxide makes bleach ($\text{NaClO}$) used for textiles, paper and disinfectants.
options.B: CFCs are chlorofluorocarbons, made from chlorine and fluorine, not bromine. They were used as refrigerants and aerosols before ozone depletion concerns.
options.C: Correct. Bromine compounds are widely used as flame retardants in plastics and fabrics, and brominated halons are used in some fire extinguishers because they interrupt combustion reactions.
options.D: PVC is poly(chloroethene), also called polychloroethene, so it is made from the chlorine-containing monomer chloroethene. This is a major use of chlorine.
